# Noninvasive Impedance Analysis During S‐ICD Insertion Provides Justification for Defibrillation Based Testing Deferment

**Authors:** Andreas G Kontopidis; Mark É Czeisler; David H Yoo; Olivia Whittaker; Daniel C Pipilas; Theofanie Mela

**Affiliations:** 1 Boston Scientific, Marlborough, Massachusetts, USA | 2 Harvard T H Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 3 Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 4 Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 5 Tufts University School of Medicine, Boston, Massachusetts, USA

## Abstract

Following subcutaneous implantable cardioverter‐defibrillator (S‐ICD) insertion, induction of ventricular fibrillation (VF) and defibrillation threshold testing (DFT) is the standard of practice to assess system performance. In contrast, DFT testing is not routinely performed after transvenous ICD (T‐ICD) insertion, supported by literature that emphasizes negative clinical repercussions and reliability of noninvasive predictors of successful defibrillation. There is a paucity of data for both the trajectory of noninvasive low voltage (LV) impedance measurements at S‐ICD insertion through the time of potential DFT testing and for the proximity of LV impedance measurements and high voltage (HV) shock impedance from 65J DFT or 10J testing.

We aim to characterize the trend in LV impedance from initial S‐ICD connection (LV T0) to final intraprocedural impedance (LV T4) and to compare LV impedance with HV impedance.

Data from patients who underwent S‐ICD implantation between July 2022 and March 2024 were analyzed. LV impedance measurements were collected during implant and HV impedance measurements were collected if 65J DFT/10J testing was performed. Differences in mean impedances at each time point were evaluated using paired t‐tests. For those who underwent 10J or 65J DFT testing, LV impedance was compared with HV impedance.

The primary analytic sample included 53 patients, with a mean age of 51 ± 15.7 years; 16 (30.2%) were female. LV impedance decreased by a mean of 14.5 ± 9.8 ohms (18.3%; p <0.001) from S‐ICD connection (T0) to the final intraprocedural measurement, approximately 60 min postimplant (T4). Among 35 patients who underwent HV testing (65J DFT or 10J), LV impedance at T4 and HV impedance did not differ significantly (1.7 ± 6.3 ohms; p = 0.116).

Our findings demonstrate a predictable reduction in LV impedance from S‐ICD connection to subsequent intraprocedural measurements. We also found that LV impedance at LV T4, the final intraprocedural measurement, did not significantly differ from contemporaneous HV impedance. Together, these findings indicate that LV impedance at implant can be expected to decline, and that 60‐min postimplant LV impedance may reliably approximate HV impedance. Evaluation of circumstances in which LV impedance could influence the decision to perform DFT testing is warranted.

## Introduction

Transvenous implantable cardioverter defibrillators (T‐ICDs) are fundamental in the clinical management of electrical cardiovascular pathologies, as they facilitate continuous intracardiac monitoring and terminate potentially rapid‐onset and life‐threatening cardiovascular arrhythmias. Clinical workflow during implantation of T‐ICDs has evolved through efforts to accurately and noninvasively determine device placement and device functionality after implantation [1]. In the early stages of T‐ICDs in the 1980s [2], nearly all patients who received T‐ICDs immediately underwent high voltage (HV) defibrillation threshold testing (DFT), plus 3‐ to 6‐week postimplantation testing through noninvasive programmed simulation DFTs (NIPS DFTs) [1]. These tests were performed to ensure that implanted devices could appropriately detect and respond to ventricular fibrillation in the event a patient went into a life‐threatening arrhythmia outside of a controlled clinical setting [3].

Over time, progression in T‐ICD system technology, including reversible biphasic waveform shock polarity, anatomical shocking vector placement congruence, and MADIT‐RIT standardized therapy zone programing drastically increased shock conversion reliability and efficacy [4, 5]. Subsequently, T‐ICD system placement became even more reliable and predictable with the addition of novel diagnostic capabilities emerging, including noninvasive low voltage (LV) impedance measurements to provide a pseudo shock impedance metric without requiring DFTs and a HV shock. Alternatives to HV DFTs are particularly desirable given the short and long‐term negative clinical repercussions associated with DFT testing, as well as increased healthcare resource utilization and costs [1]. Encouragingly, a study of 332 patients found that the success of shocks for clinically significant arrhythmias was the same for patients who underwent full DFT (91%; n = 129) and for those who did not have any form of DFT (92%; n = 203) [1], providing evidence to support deferment of DFT testing immediately following T‐ICD implantation [6]. In response to a growing evidence base, clinical practice following T‐ICD implantation has largely shifted to deferment of DFTs and NIPS testing [3], with the exception of right sided implants, subcutaneous defibrillators, and patients at higher risk [7]. DFT testing is based on probabilistic values, but DFT testing is no longer routinely recommended in patients undergoing left‐sided T‐ICD implantation. This has in turn decreased the clinical application of HV impedance as a surrogate for successful DFT testing in T‐ICDs, however, the association of HV impedance during Emblem Subcutaneous ICD (S‐ICD) insertions is still under investigation [3].

In comparison to postimplantation DFT testing for T‐ICDs, less evidence exists for DFT testing with S‐ICD, for which clinical practice includes DFT testing post‐implant in the vast majority of cases [3], and is still the device manufacturer recommendation [8]. Attempts to utilize acute lower energy shocks to determine HV impedance and DFT conversion probability have been made, including a study that shows no statistical difference in conversion probability between less energy shocks (10J) to full energy shocks (80J) at the time of implant [9]. Continuing this precedent, the need for further investigation regarding the use of noninvasive LV metrics as an HV impedance surrogate is of clinical importance for S‐ICD implant technique progression, and DFT testing deferment. Lack of this evidence is partly due to the novelty of the system and to its unique implant technique, which avoids all transvenous access sites to provide defibrillation therapy via entirely extra‐thoracic placement. To achieve this goal, the S‐ICD provides a larger therapy output of 80J vs the transvenous 41J standard, requiring an increased size of the device. Since its adoption, implant techniques, studies, and technological advancements have led to significant evolution of the S‐ICD system [10]. Previously recommended 3‐incision techniques with the defibrillating coil placed left lateral of the sternum and subcutaneous pocket formation have now transitioned to an intermuscular pocket formation between the serratus and latissimus dorsi, and a 2‐incision technique with heightened focused on reducing depth of adipose tissue between the coil and sternum in a more medial position to mitigate propagation of myopotentials in the context of an indexed PRAETORIAN score [11]. These procedural improvements have led to lower impedance values, lower inappropriate shock rates, and more optimal sensing, with comparable clinical results to T‐ICDs demonstrated through the PRAETORIAN and ATLAS trials [12].

Much like improvements throughout the longevity of T‐ICD system placements, improvements of the S‐ICD system have led to increased confidence and predictability in anatomical vector positioning of the S‐ICD system, leading to higher shock conversion efficacy [13]. Device algorithms and diagnostic features have also progressed; the SMART pass filter algorithm introduced in 2016, which was followed with the UNTOUCHED and EFFORTLESS clinical trials, found noninferiority in inappropriate shock rates and lead related complication rates compared to T‐ICDs [12].

Most recently, in 2022, the MILAN update provided a novel noninvasive diagnostic capability of LV impedance measurements, like that of T‐ICDs. In the wake of these advancements in predictability of conversion success due to procedural improvements, algorithm enhancements, and clinical trials; exploration of the potential for minimizing DFT testing for the S‐ICD system is warranted. To date, the evidence base consists primarily of the EMILY abstract, which reported findings from 41 patients who underwent S‐ICD implantation with MILAN LV impedance measurements. The investigators found that LV impedances were within 10 ohms of HV shock impedances in 83% of patients, with a strong correlation overall (Pearson r = 0.889) [14]. Given that patients with below 90‐ohm HV impedance have a greater than 90% probability of S‐ICD DFT conversion success [14, 15], and that univariate analysis has demonstrated that HV impedance values above 138 ohms predict high DFT test values and low conversion probability [16], accurate LV impedance measurements with meaningful correlation to the HV impedance has prognostic value [17]. Further assessment of MILAN LV impedance measurements in larger clinical samples with more comprehensive characterization of measurements, including temporal trends, is necessary to provide insights into the accuracy of the LV impedance measurements and how they may be used in clinical practice. We therefore sought to characterize the trend in LV impedance from initial connection of device (LV T0) to final intraprocedural impedance (LV T4), and to further correlate LV impedance with HV shock impedance.

## Methods

This was a retrospective observational study within Massachusetts General Brigham (MGB) care centers in the United States. Eligible participants included patients who had received a newly implanted S‐ICD following the implementation of the March 2022 MILAN upgrade, after which time LV impedance measurements were made available through the device. All consecutive patients that underwent S‐ICD insertion between July 2022 and March 2024 at Massachusetts General Hospital were included in this study, with no exclusion upon later review. Impedance measurements were documented day of S‐ICD insertion to avoid potential residual confounding from retrospective analysis.

All study data, including age, sex, body mass index (BMI), S‐ICD implantation date, intermuscular or subcutaneous pocket formation, intraoperative LV impedance measurements (timepoints relative to device implantation: T0 [0 m], T1 [5 m], T2 [10 m], T3 [30 m], T4 [60 m]), 10J HV impedance, and 65J DFT HV impedance were extracted from the electronic medical record using Massachusetts General Hospital's D4Q clinical data warehouse. LV impedance measurements are generated by the S‐ICD system through administration of a sub‐threshold 4 V output at 2 µs to generate a pseudo shock impedance value of proximity to that generated from a HV (10J or 65J DFT) therapy. A variable of HV impedance was created with 65J DFT testing, or with a 10J shock if conducted, since there is evidence of no statistically significant differences in the average impedance values between the two [9].

Data from patients who met the inclusion criteria during the study were included and comprised the primary analytic sample. Two additional subsamples were created: (1) patients who underwent HV testing (HV subsample) and (2) patients who had measures at all timepoints and underwent DFT testing. Because collection of these measurements was not mutually exclusive, data from patients could be present in all three samples.

For the primary analysis, descriptive statistics were used to characterize the absolute and relative trends of intraprocedural LV impedance measurements (T0 through T4), including mean ± SD among all patients as well as absolute and relative delta impedance, defined as change in within‐participant measurements of post‐implant impedance at T0 and each of T1 through T4. For each comparison, paired t‐tests were used to identify statistically significant difference in delta impedance. Linear regression modeling was used to assess for a statistically significant relationship between LV impedance measurements at T0 as the explanatory variable and at T4, the last intraprocedural measure, as the dependent variable. Models were constructed as univariate for the primary analysis and multivariate, with age, sex, BMI, and pocket formation as covariates.

Within the HV subsample, descriptive statistics were used to compare high voltage testing impedance measures with T0 and T4, respectively. Paired t‐tests were used to compare delta impedances, and univariate and multivariate regression models were used with HV impedance measures as dependent variables and T0 and T4 as independent variables in separate models. The percentage of intraprocedural impedance measures within 5 or 10 ohms of HV testing measures was also calculated. For exploratory analyses, intraprocedural LV impedance measurements were compared by age (categorized), sex, BMI, and pocket formation in the primary analytic sample.

As these data were generated through standard clinical operations, specific informed consent for this study protocol was not required. The protocol was reviewed by the Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Boards and met criteria for exemption (45 CFR 46) as a secondary research protocol. Analyses were conducted using Python software (version 3.8.8; Python Software Foundation) using the statsmodels module (version 0.12.2). A p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

## Results

Between July 2022 and March 2024, 53 patients underwent new S‐ICD implantation, of whom 35 (66.0%) underwent HV testing (i.e., 10J shocks, 65J DFT testing, or both) (Table 1). Among patients comprising the primary analytic sample, the mean ± SD age was 51 ± 15.7 years, and 16 (30.2%) were of female sex. Categorized BMI across the sample was distributed with 15 (28.3%) having healthy BMI, 23 (43.4%) overweight BMI, and 15 (28.3%) obese BMI. Descriptive statistics for the HV subsample were numerically similar to those of the primary analytic sample.

In the primary analytic sample, mean ± SD LV impedance decreased sequentially with time from implant, ranging from 79.5 ± 22.5 ohms at T0 to 65.0 ± 16.4 ohms at T4 (Table 2). Within‐patient analyses of absolute differences in impedance demonstrated that compared with LV impedance at T0, measures at each subsequent timepoint (T1 through T4) were significantly lower, with a mean absolute difference of −5.2 ± 3.9 ohms at T1 versus T0 and a mean absolute difference of −14.5 ± 9.8 ohms at T4 versus T0 (both p < 0.001). Similar results were observed for relative differences in LV impedance. For example, the mean relative difference at T1 versus T0 was −6.5% ± 5.0% and at T4 versus T0 was −18.3% ± 7.0% (both p < 0.001).

Individual‐level line plots of intraprocedural LV impedance from T0 through T4 are plotted in Figure 1. Univariate linear regression modeling with T0 as the explanatory variable and T4 as the dependent variable produced the following fitted regression model: LV T4 = 11.4516 + 0.6733 × LV T0. The overall regression was statistically significant (R 2 = 0.843, F(1, 51) = 279.8, p < 0.001), with T0 significantly predicting T4 (β [95% CI] = 0.67 [0.59 to 0.75], p < 0.001). Multivariate regression modeling with T0, age, sex, BMI, and pocket formation as explanatory variables and T4 as the dependent variable also yielded a model with T0 statistically significantly predicting T4 (β [95% CI] = 0.66 [0.57 to 0.75], p <0.001), while none of age, sex, BMI, or pocket formation were significant predictors (p ≥ 0.126).

Comparing LV and HV impedance among patients with both values, only 9 out of 35 (25.7%) LV impedances taken at T0 were within 10 ohms of HV impedances, whereas 31 out of 35 (88.6%) LV and HV impedances taken at T4 were within 10 ohms of each other (Figure 2). Within the HV subsample, univariate regression modeling was performed with each of T0 and T4 as explanatory variables and HV testing as the dependent variable. Both models were statistically significant. The model with T4 as an explanatory variable had a higher coefficient of determination, with β [95% CI] = 0.93 [0.78 to 1.09] (p <0.001) and R 2 = 0.816, compared with the model with T0 as the explanatory variable (β [95% CI] = 0.60 [0.48 to 0.72], p < 0.001; R 2 = 0.753).

Findings from exploratory analyses of LV impedance measurements by patient age category, sex, BMI category, and intermuscular versus subcutaneous S‐ICD pocket formation are reported in the Supplementary Materials (Tables S1–S4). LV impedance measurements were statistically significantly higher at T0 through T4 among patients with obese BMIs compared to patients with healthy BMIs (p ≤ 0.041).

## Discussion

In this retrospective study of 53 S‐ICD recipients, we found that LV impedance measurements decreased by nearly 20% on average in the hour following S‐ICD implantation, and that this decline leads to convergence of LV and HV impedance measurements one‐hour post‐implantation. As a result, whereas only one‐quarter of LV measurements obtained immediately post‐implant were within 10 ohms of HV measurements, nearly 90% of LV measurements obtained one‐hour post‐implant from the same patients were within this range. Together, these findings reveal a characterizable temporal trend of LV impedance measurements and indicate that LV measurements may approximate HV measurements after a decline post‐implantation. While the technical and patient factors underlying this decline require further investigation, the predictability of S‐ICD intraprocedural LV impedance trends and its association with HV impedance is of clinical importance, as its exploration as a reliable metric could impact decision‐making on DFT deferment following S‐ICD implantation.

Technical factors related to the S‐ICD implantation process could influence the trajectory of LV impedance values. For example, air entrapment and inappropriate electrode contact with adipose tissue may diminish the accuracy of LV system impedance measurements [18]. Air entrapment was an early cause of inappropriate S‐ICD function due to intermittent and transient effects of the entrapped air on the sensing process. It is plausible that the prevalence of undetected acute and transient air entrapment in the subcutaneous space is high, with large‐volume physiologic absorption and resolution of residual air immediately post‐implantation with continued gradual reabsorption at a lower rate thereafter, as evidenced by 99% resolution of entrapped air within one week of the procedure based on computed tomography imaging [19]. The considerable decline in entrapped air in the immediate post‐implant phase could partially account for the high‐magnitude reduction in LV measures.

Pocket formation and tunneling from the xiphoid incision to the pocket, as well as superiorly up the sternum, introduces the potential for multiple air tracts in adipose tissue, limiting optimal electrode contact with the tissue, reducing LV impedance accuracy. Specifically, effective defibrillation is based on delivery of an electrical shock to a critical amount of myocardial cells, which is determined by the flow of electrical current and resistance on the circuit [20]. The impact optimal electrode contact can have on defibrillation success can be appreciated when considering conventional, hand‐held defibrillator paddles, where increases in pressure force increases electrode‐skin contact levels while decreasing air volume in the lungs, thus, requiring different paddle forces for adults as compared with children [20]. One possible approach to further accelerate this air dispersion could be the administration of saline within the sheath of the delivery system, prior to introducing the electrode. Following the insertion of the electrode, massaging the sternum to disperse residual air entrapment created during tunneling and utilizing saline's conductive properties could accelerate the LV impedance trajectory by providing better electrode contact. Further investigation is required to analyze the effect air dispersion and fluid dynamics have on the rate and absolute value of intraprocedural LV system impedance measurements during S‐ICD implantation.

Our exploratory findings comparing subcutaneous versus intermuscular device placement suggest that while the rate of regression of impedance from initial connection of the device to final closure did not change between pocket formation groups, the intermuscular pocket formation group, which is found deeper in the body tucked between muscle groups, could be associated with overall lower LV impedance values. In one study with more than 1500 patients, patients with intermuscular pocket formation showed lower inappropriate shock rates compared to that of subcutaneous pocket formation, indicating precedent for pocket formations influencing system performance [21]. More research is required to determine statistical significance of LV impedance values and trends for differing pocket formations, specifically, within the scope of temporal air entrapment dissipation as well as device‐skin electrode contact. Aside from air entrapment and pocket formation; device temperature, as the device equilibrates from its storage to body temperature, could play a role in optimizing electrode contact and accuracy of intraprocedural LV impedance trends and values [18]. Dense fibrous encapsulation has been reported post S‐ICD system implantation, leading to high HV impedance values and failed DFT testing [16]. Additional studies report long‐term impedance rise post S‐ICD implant, along with the impact revascularized device pouches may have on mitigating capsule formation and reducing impedance values [22]. Our study did not investigate long‐term outcomes, and further studies are needed to determine whether acute DFT testing has any correlation with capsule formation and long‐term impedance trends.

Patient factors such as BMI, sex, and age could also be influential in the decline and absolute values of intraprocedural S‐ICD impedances from the time of device connection to final closure. A positive correlation between high BMI and high DFT has been demonstrated in previous studies [23]. The elevated DFT in obese patients could be related to the presence of increased adipose tissue, which is a poor electrical conductor. Studies have shown that during an 80J cardioversion administered by the S‐ICD system, varying electrical conductivity within different tissue densities, such as adipose tissue, will inherently have higher resistance to electrical conductivity, compared to less dense parts of the body such as bone [23, 24]. Our exploratory analysis findings were concurrent with this precedent; however, larger patient populations are required to have sufficiently powered testing for statistically significant differences.

Patients with BMI classification of obese had statistically significant higher T0 and T4 values, as well as a larger overage decrease from T0 to T4, compared to BMI's classified as healthy or overweight. During S‐ICD electrode implantation, any increased amount of adipose between the sternum and electrode has shown to increase system impedance [24]. More investigation is required, specifically, targeting the impact increased adipose tissue directly above the sternum has on intraprocedural LV impedance values and its trends. These exploratory findings indicate that the excess adipose tissue in obese BMI patients could be associated with overall higher intraprocedural LV impedance measurements.

Aside from BMI, patient factors such as sex and age could play an influence on the intraprocedural and long‐term LV impedance measurements. Previous studies have indicated that female LV impedances were significantly associated with increased impedance over >2 year periods post procedurally [22]. In our exploratory findings, males reported higher mean T0 and T4 LV impedance values compared to females, however, larger patient populations are required for statistical significance. Aside from operator technique to ensure optimal S‐ICD system placement, patient factors such as BMI, sex, age, and perhaps scar tissue and septal/posterior wall thickness, require further analysis to determine their impact on intraprocedural LV impedance trends and absolute values.

Beyond patient and technical factors that influence intraprocedural LV and HV impedance values, S‐ICD system DFT conversion probability is also influenced by anatomical system placement. Relative to the T‐ICD system, the S‐ICD system lacks the breadth of randomized controlled trials and studies that identify potential markers of DFT conversion success. For example, there is a significant impact of anatomical lead placement, specifically aligning the shocking vector with the apex of the heart when evaluating conversion probability [13]. The T‐ICD shocking vector must transverse directly through myocardial tissue within the heart, which is historically susceptible to variance among LV mass between ischemic and nonischemic hearts [25]. Conversely, the S‐ICD system avoids the vasculature and heart entirely and sits subcutaneously above the sternum in adipose tissue. Encouragingly, PRAETORIAN scores have been validated for the implantation of the S‐ICD system, in which LV mass does not appear to be a factor for successful DFTs [11]. The difference of surrounding myocardial (T‐ICDs) versus adipose (S‐ICDs) tissue, and respective shocking vector relationship, could influence conversion probability success, even with adequate HV and LV impedance values. More studies, specifically with the S‐ICD system, are required to determine if these associated factors outside of impedance values influence conversion probability.

Strengths of this study include the novel findings of a characterizable regression in impedance from connection of the device to final intraprocedural measurements, as well as an augmented correlation between LV and HV impedance measurements previously investigated. These findings further strengthen the utility of LV impedance measurements at the time of S‐ICD system insertion as a modality to accurately assess system integrity and influence DFT testing deferment in clinical practice in the scope of patient safety and procedural efficiency.

Limitations of the study include the lack of a demographically representative sample as well as a small cell count, specifically, for the HV impedance analytic group (N = 35) and within exploratory subgroup analysis (BMI, sex, age, and pocket formation) for statistical significance. Similarly, a larger patient population would aid in strengthening the findings of regression of LV impedances within the primary analytic group (N = 53), although the patient population in this group did meet our power analysis requirements. LV impedances collected by the S‐ICD system have lower resolution (range of 5 ohms per data collection) compared to that of HV impedances (range of 1 ohm per data point), decreasing confidence intervals of LV to HV comparisons. Retrospective studies are observational and subject to bias due to unmeasured confounding, so the findings in this manuscript are correlational rather than causal. Future studies designed for causal analysis could test the hypotheses generated from this study. Additionally, time intervals utilized in this study (T0–T4) were developed to normalize for operator and implant time. The closing process for the SICD generator has variability between implanters. Factors associated with this variability include the decision to tie down the device to the pocket, the number of layers to close, and if/when DFT testing is performed. The variability of these factors will have an influence on the time to final closure of the pocket and the normalization of the time intervals utilized in this study (T0–T4).

In conclusion, the results of our primary analytic sample (N = 53) demonstrate a predictable regression in LV impedance (14.5 ± 9.8 ohms, p < 0.001; −18.3%, p < 0.001) from first connection of device, T0, to subsequent final intraprocedural measurements, T4. High voltage subgroup analysis (N = 35) found a statistically significant correlation between LV T4, the final intraprocedural low voltage impedance, and HV shock impedances impedance (−1.7 ± 6.3 ohms; p = 0.116; −2.2%, p = 0.19). This study showed a characterizable regression of intraoperative LV impedances, while further correlating LV impedances with HV impedance. This strengthened correlation, in unison with existing HV impedance precedent, allows for the opportunity for noninvasive LV impedances to be considered in the decision making of procedural DFT testing. Initiatives for utilizing lower energy 10J shocks as a replacement for DFT testing have already taken form [9]; however, official recommendations by the device manufacturer are still to perform DFT tests post implantation of S‐ICD system insertion [8]. More studies are required to further strengthen the clinical trajectory of utilizing lower energy or potentially noninvasive LV impedance metrics as a modality to justify the deferment of DFT testing. DFT testing has been shown to have negative long‐term patient safety repercussions, increase in acute procedural risks, as well as an increase burden on hospital resources, time, and procedural efficiency [1].
